books.section: Topic 4.8 Jackson and Federal Power, A. The Second Two-Party System: The Democrats and the Whigs

stimulus.text: Published in 1832, the cartoon shows President Andrew Jackson in a crown and royal robes, holding a scepter in one hand and a scroll labeled "VETO" in the other. He stands on torn papers, including one labeled "CONSTITUTION of the UNITED STATES." The caption reads "KING ANDREW THE FIRST."
stimulus.source_note: Political cartoon "King Andrew the First," published 1832, artist unknown (Library of Congress). Public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The cartoonist's portrait of Jackson as a king most directly criticizes which of the following?

options.text: Jackson's support for the spoils system
options.misconception: The spoils system is the most famous Jackson practice, so it is easy to pick it for any attack on Jackson.

options.text: Jackson's frequent use of the presidential veto

options.misconception: Internal improvements were a Whig cause, so Jackson's enemies attacked him for opposing them, not for supporting them.

options.text: Jackson's opposition to the protective tariff
options.misconception: The tariff was a big fight of the era, so it is easy to blame every Jackson cartoon on it.

rationales.A: The spoils system put supporters in office, but the cartoon shows a veto scroll, not officeholders.
rationales.B: The scroll in Jackson's hand reads 'VETO,' and the crown and robes turn his vetoes into the acts of a king.
rationales.C: Jackson opposed federal spending on internal improvements, and the cartoon does not show him building anything.
rationales.D: Jackson signed the Tariff of 1832, and the cartoon's charge is about his vetoes, not the tariff.
rationales.general:
1. Look at what Jackson holds. The scroll in his left hand reads 'VETO,' and he wears a crown and royal robes.
2. Ask what the symbols charge him with. A king rules alone, so the cartoon says Jackson's vetoes made him rule like a monarch.
Background: Jackson vetoed 12 bills, more than the 10 vetoed by all his predecessors combined.
Remember: a cartoon's props name its charge, so read the scroll before you read the crown.

figures.caption: King Andrew the First, 1832. Jackson in crown and robes, holding a veto scroll.
figures.alt: A political cartoon of President Andrew Jackson in a crown and royal robes, holding a scepter and a scroll labeled VETO, standing on torn papers including the Constitution
